question: Second-generation antihistamines such as fexofenadine avoid causing sedation because they are structurally unable to bind to H1 receptors in the brain.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Second-generation antihistamines are structurally capable of binding central H1 receptors — they are inverse agonists with similar receptor affinity. They avoid sedation because they are substrates for P-glycoprotein efflux pumps at the blood-brain barrier, which actively pump them out of the CNS. This is a pharmacokinetic distinction (distribution), not a pharmacodynamic one.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this is a common misconception. Second-generation antihistamines CAN bind central H1 receptors if they reach the brain. They avoid sedation primarily because they are substrates of P-glycoprotein efflux pumps at the blood-brain barrier, which actively transport them back into the bloodstream before they accumulate in the CNS. The distinction is pharmacokinetic (reduced brain entry), not pharmacodynamic (receptor binding affinity).
